tool.name: GraphQL
tool.tagline: Typed query language for APIs: clients ask for exactly the data they need
tool.description: GraphQL is a query language and runtime for APIs: a server publishes a typed schema, and clients send queries that name exactly the fields they want, getting back JSON in the same shape. It is used by web and mobile teams to fetch nested data in one round trip, evolve APIs without versioning, and give frontends a self-documenting contract.

glossary.def: In GraphQL, the text a client sends listing exactly the data it wants back; also the name of the read-only kind of operation.
The braces in a GraphQL query that list which fields you want from an object.
The name you give a query or mutation, like CurrentUser, so servers and tools can recognise it.
A GraphQL operation that changes data, such as creating an order; written like a query but starting with mutation.
A GraphQL operation that stays open and receives a new result every time a matching event happens, such as a new chat message.
A web page for writing and trying GraphQL queries, with field suggestions and documentation taken from the schema.
Schema Definition Language: GraphQL's short notation for writing a schema, e.g. type Book { title: String! }.
One of the starting points of a GraphQL schema, Query, Mutation or Subscription; every request begins at one of their fields.
A GraphQL type with named fields, like Book with title and pages.
A GraphQL type marked with ! (like String!), promising the value is never null.
A GraphQL type declared with input that groups the values passed as one argument, like the details of a new book.
An instruction starting with @ attached to part of a GraphQL query or schema, such as @skip or @deprecated.
The function a GraphQL server runs to produce one field's value, e.g. looking up a book's author.
The resolver GraphQL uses when you haven't written one: it reads the property with the field's name from the parent object.
The part of a GraphQL server that walks a query, calls the resolvers and assembles the response.
A named, reusable list of fields on one type that queries can include with ...Name.
A ... on Type { } block in a query that selects some fields only when the object is that exact type.
In GraphQL, a new name for a field in the response, e.g. small: avatar(size: 64), so the same field can be asked for twice.
Keeping each screen component's GraphQL fragment next to the code that displays those fields.
The key a field's result appears under in GraphQL's JSON answer: the field name, or its alias.
In GraphQL, a type listing fields that several object types share; each type that implements it must have those fields.
A GraphQL type whose value is one of several listed object types that need not share fields, e.g. User | Post.
A GraphQL response with some data plus an errors list, because only some fields failed.
When a non-null GraphQL field fails, its null moves up to the nearest parent that may be null, erasing that parent's other fields too.
Asking a GraphQL server, with a built-in query, to describe its own schema; tools use it for autocomplete and documentation.
A client-side store that keeps each fetched object once, filed by its type and id, so every screen showing it updates together.
Fetching a list with one query and then each item's related data with one more query per item: N+1 queries instead of 2.
A small library that collects the keys resolvers ask for at about the same time and loads them in one batch, remembering results for one request.
The function you give DataLoader: it takes a list of keys and returns the matching values in the same order.
An opaque string marking a position in a list, which a client passes back to get the items after (or before) it.
A standard GraphQL shape for paginated lists: edges with a cursor and node each, plus pageInfo saying whether more pages exist.
A GraphQL input type marked @oneOf: the caller must fill in exactly one of its fields.
Abstract syntax tree: text such as code or a query turned into a tree of objects a program can inspect and change.
The step of GraphQL execution that gathers a selection's fields, merging fragments and fields with the same response key.
An estimate of how much work a GraphQL query will cause, from field weights multiplied by list sizes, used to reject heavy queries.
GraphQL operations registered ahead of time, so the server runs only those, identified by their hash.
Splitting one GraphQL API across many services: each team's subgraph owns some types, and a router combines them for clients.
In GraphQL federation, one team's GraphQL service, declaring the types and fields it owns.
In GraphQL federation, the single combined schema that clients query, built from all the subgraphs.
In GraphQL federation, a type identified by a key (like upc) that several subgraphs add fields to.

concepts.name: What GraphQL is
concepts.summary: Ask a server for exactly the data you need, in one request, and get back JSON shaped like your question.
concepts.why: Knowing what GraphQL solves (and what it costs) tells you when to choose it over a classic REST API.
concepts.body:
Apps constantly need data that lives somewhere else. A weather app asks a weather company's computers for today's forecast; a shop's web page asks its server for your basket. The program that asks is the **client**; the program that answers is the server you met in Node.js.

The set of requests a server agrees to answer, and how to phrase them, is its **API** (application programming interface). Think of a restaurant menu: you can only order what's on it, and only in the way it describes.

The most common style of web API is **REST**. The server offers many URLs, and each one, called an **endpoint**, returns a fixed bundle of data. `/users/42` returns everything about user 42 whether you need it or not, and getting their posts means a second request to `/users/42/posts`.

**GraphQL** is a different way to build an API. It usually has a single URL, often `/graphql`. The client sends a **query**: a short text listing exactly the pieces of data it wants. Each named piece, like a user's `name`, is a **field**. The answer is JSON in the same shape as the query.

The server publishes a **schema**: the complete, typed list of what can be asked for — every kind of object, its fields, and whether each holds text, a number, true/false or another object. Because the schema exists, tools can check a query before it runs, suggest field names as you type, and catch typos immediately.

Two everyday problems disappear. A small phone screen and a big desktop page can ask the same API for different fields, so nobody downloads data they won't show (over-fetching). And nested data, such as a user plus their posts, arrives in one **round trip** — one request and its reply — instead of several (under-fetching).

GraphQL is a specification, a written rulebook, not a product: graphql-js is the official JavaScript version, and servers exist for every major language. It has costs too. Ordinary web caching is harder because almost every request goes to the same URL, and a carelessly designed schema lets a client ask for an enormous amount of data at once.
takeaways: A GraphQL API has one URL and one typed schema; clients pick the fields
The JSON response has the same shape as the query, under `data`
It's a specification; graphql-js is the official JavaScript implementation
pitfalls: Thinking GraphQL is a database language: it sits in front of any data — databases, files or other APIs.

quiz.q: What problem does letting clients pick their fields mainly solve?
options: Getting too much or too little data per request
quiz.explain: Clients get exactly the fields they ask for, nested data included, in one round trip.

concepts.name: Queries and fields
concepts.summary: Write queries as nested lists of fields in braces, and give each one a name so it's easy to recognise later.
concepts.why: Every GraphQL interaction starts with reading and writing query documents.
concepts.body:
A GraphQL query is written as a **document**: plain text you send to the server. Its core is a **selection set**, a pair of braces listing the fields you want.

Some fields hold one plain value: a string, a number, true/false, an ID, or one choice from a fixed list of options such as `DRAFT` or `PUBLISHED` (a type like that is called an **enum**). Single values like these are **scalars**, and they are the leaves of the tree.

Other fields hold an object, such as a user or a team. Those must get their own selection set, because GraphQL never sends "the whole object" unless you list the fields you want from it.

```graphql
query CurrentUser {
  me {
    name
    avatarUrl
    team { name }
  }
}
```

Pieces of a document:

- **Operation type**: `query` (read data), `mutation` (change data) or `subscription` (receive live updates); later lessons cover the last two. The shorthand `{ ... }` is an unnamed query.
- **Operation name**: `CurrentUser` above. Always name operations in real code: the server can record which named operation ran, and client tools use the name to keep track of results.
- **Fields** can take arguments, e.g. `posts(first: 5)`; a later lesson covers them.
- `__typename` can be requested on any object to learn its exact type, such as `"User"`.

A document may contain several operations; the request then says which one to run via `operationName`.

Before running anything, the server checks the document against the schema. Asking for a field that doesn't exist, or for an object field without a selection set, is a **validation error**: the whole operation is rejected and none of the server's code runs. This is one of GraphQL's best features. Typos are caught at once, and GraphiQL (a web page for trying out queries) suggests field names as you type.
takeaways: Object fields need a selection set; scalars are the leaves
Name every operation so it's easy to recognise on the server and in tools
Unknown fields are rejected before anything runs
pitfalls: Expecting `{ me }` to return the entire user object.

quiz.q: Why does `query { me }` fail when `me` returns a User object?
quiz.explain: GraphQL never returns an object implicitly; you must select its fields.

concepts.name: Schema definition language
concepts.summary: Write a schema in SDL: object types, the five built-in scalars, enums, lists, and the `!` that means "never null".
concepts.why: The schema is the contract that every client and every server tool relies on.
concepts.body:
Schemas are written in a short notation called the **Schema Definition Language (SDL)**. Every query starts from one of three special **root types**: `Query` for reading, `Mutation` for changing data and `Subscription` for live updates. Every other type is reached through their fields.

```graphql
type Query { book(id: ID!): Book  books: [Book!]! }
type Book { id: ID!  title: String!  pages: Int  genre: Genre }
enum Genre { FICTION  SCIENCE  HISTORY }
```

The building blocks:

- **Scalars**: `Int` (whole numbers up to about ±2 billion), `Float` (numbers with decimals), `String`, `Boolean`, `ID` (sent as a string, meant for identifiers). Servers can add their own scalars, like `DateTime`.
- **Object types** have fields; each field has a type and optional arguments.
- **Enums** restrict a value to a fixed set of names.
- **Lists** `[T]` hold many values of type `T`, and **non-null** `T!` promises the value is never `null`.

Where you put `!` matters: `[Book!]!` means the list itself is never null and contains no null items; `[Book]` allows both a null list and null items.

A field that may be `null` is called **nullable**, and fields are nullable by default. That's deliberate: if producing one field's value fails, the server can return `null` for just that field and still deliver the rest of the answer. Mark a field `!` only when you can always produce it.

Descriptions are written as strings before a definition (`"The book's ISBN-13"`) and show up in documentation tools such as GraphiQL.
takeaways: Every query starts at a root type: Query, Mutation or Subscription
Five built-in scalars: Int, Float, String, Boolean, ID
Fields are nullable by default; `!` makes a promise
pitfalls: Marking everything non-null, so one failing field wipes out its whole parent object.

quiz.q: Which value is NOT allowed for a field of type `[String!]`?
quiz.explain: The items are non-null, so a null item is invalid; the list itself may be null.

concepts.name: Arguments and variables
concepts.summary: Pass arguments to fields, and supply their values through typed variables instead of pasting them into the query text.
concepts.why: Variables make operations reusable and stop users from smuggling extra query text into them.
concepts.body:
Any field can declare **arguments**, e.g. `book(id: ID!)` or `books(genre: Genre, first: Int = 10)`. Arguments can have default values in the schema.

Typing values straight into the query text works while you explore, but real clients use **variables**: the operation declares typed placeholders, and the values travel separately as JSON.

```graphql
query Book($id: ID!, $withReviews: Boolean = false) {
  book(id: $id) { title }
}
```

The HTTP request then carries `{"query": "...", "variables": {"id": "b1"}}`.

Why this matters:

- The query text never changes, so the server and tools can store it, cache it and recognise it by its operation name.
- Values are checked against their declared types. You never glue user-typed text into a query string, so nobody can sneak extra query text in through a form field (an **injection** bug).
- A variable's type must fit where it's used: `$id: ID` (nullable) can't be passed to an `ID!` argument unless it has a default.

Complex arguments use **input types**, declared with `input` instead of `type`. Input types may only contain scalars, enums and other input types, never ordinary object types.

**Directives** are instructions starting with `@`. Two built-in ones, `@include(if: $flag)` and `@skip(if: $flag)`, let a variable switch parts of a selection on or off.
takeaways: Declare `$vars` with types in the operation, send values as JSON
Never build a query by gluing in text a user typed
Complex arguments use `input` types
`@include` / `@skip` toggle fields from variables
pitfalls: Passing a nullable variable to a non-null argument without a default; validation rejects it.

quiz.q: Why should clients send values as variables rather than inlining them?
options: The query text stays constant and values are typed
quiz.explain: A query text that never changes can be cached and stored, and variables are checked against their types.

concepts.name: Mutations
concepts.summary: Change data with mutation fields that take one input object and return a result object the client can read back.
concepts.why: Writes in GraphQL follow conventions that keep clients' caches up to date.
concepts.body:
A **mutation** is an operation that changes data: it creates an order, renames a file, cancels a booking. It is written just like a query but starts with `mutation`, and its fields live on the `Mutation` root type.

```graphql
type Mutation {
  addBook(input: AddBookInput!): AddBookPayload!
}
input AddBookInput { title: String!  authorId: ID! }
type AddBookPayload { book: Book  errors: [UserError!]! }
```

Conventions worth adopting:

- Name mutations as verbs for specific actions (`publishPost`, `cancelOrder`) rather than one generic `updatePost` with dozens of optional fields.
- Take a single `input` argument of an input type, so you can add fields later without breaking existing callers.
- Return a **payload** type: an object holding the result of the change, such as the new or updated book. The client picks fields on it, like in any query.
- Treat failures you expect as part of the business — a badly formed email, "out of stock" — as data in the payload, and keep the top-level `errors` list for real breakdowns.

Why return the changed object? Client libraries such as Apollo, urql and Relay keep a local copy of every object they've fetched, filed by its `id`. When a mutation returns an object with an `id`, they update that copy automatically, so the screen shows the change without another request.

One rule differs from queries: when a document has several top-level mutation fields, they run **one after another, in order**, while a query's top-level fields may run at the same time.
takeaways: Top-level mutation fields run one after another, in document order
One `input` argument plus a payload type is the common convention
Return changed objects with ids so client caches update
pitfalls: Returning only true/false, forcing the client to fetch again whatever changed.

quiz.q: Two root fields in one mutation document are executed how?
quiz.explain: The spec requires top-level mutation fields to run one after another, in the order written.

concepts.name: Resolvers: serving a schema
concepts.summary: Implement a schema with resolver functions that receive parent, args, context and info, and return values or promises.
concepts.why: Resolvers are where a GraphQL server actually fetches data.
concepts.body:
A server pairs the schema with **resolvers**: one function per field that produces its value. Most JavaScript servers (Apollo Server, GraphQL Yoga, graphql-tools) take an object of resolvers, grouped by type name and then by field name.

Each resolver receives four arguments:

- `parent`: the value returned by the parent field's resolver (the book, when resolving `Book.author`).
- `args`: the field's arguments, already checked and converted to their declared types.
- `context`: an object you create fresh for every request, holding things like the logged-in user and a database connection.
- `info`: details about the current field and query (used by advanced tools).

A resolver may return a value or a promise; the GraphQL engine (the **executor**) waits for it. Fields without a resolver use the **default resolver**, which reads the property of the same name from `parent`. So you only write resolvers where your stored data differs from the schema.

Execution walks the query from the top down: resolve `Query.book`, then for that book resolve `title` and `author`, and so on. Each result is then **completed**: checked against the field's type, with lists handled item by item and the non-null rules enforced.

Keep resolvers thin. Deciding what the logged-in user may see or change is called **authorization**; put those checks, and the code that reads the database, in separate plain functions that the resolver calls. Then REST endpoints, scheduled background tasks and GraphQL all share the same rules.
takeaways: Resolver signature: (parent, args, context, info)
Return values or promises; the executor waits for them
The default resolver reads `parent[fieldName]`
Put per-request things (the user, loaders) in context
pitfalls: Storing per-request data in module-level variables, so one user's data leaks to the next.

options: The Book object returned by the parent field
quiz.explain: Each resolver receives the value its parent field produced.

concepts.name: Fragments, aliases and directives
concepts.summary: Reuse selections with fragments, rename or repeat fields with aliases, and keep each screen part's data needs next to its code.
concepts.why: Fragments are how real client apps keep large queries maintainable.
concepts.body:
A **fragment** is a named, reusable selection on a type:

```graphql
fragment BookCard on Book { id title cover { url } }
query { featured { ...BookCard }  recent { ...BookCard } }
```

Fragments let each piece of the screen (each UI component) declare the fields it displays, right next to its own code; this is called **colocation**. The page's query then spreads (`...`) the fragments of the components it contains. Relay and Apollo Client build features on exactly this.

**Aliases** rename a field in the response. They are required when you request the same field twice with different arguments, because both results would otherwise land on the same JSON key (the **response key**):

```graphql
{ small: avatar(size: 64) { url }  large: avatar(size: 512) { url } }
```

**Inline fragments** `... on Type { }` select fields only when the object turns out to be that exact type; the next lesson uses them with types that can hold several kinds of object.

The built-in directives `@include(if:)` and `@skip(if:)` toggle selections, `@deprecated` marks parts of the schema as on their way out, and `@specifiedBy` links to the rules for a custom scalar. Servers may define their own directives.

Validation checks that every fragment is used, that each spread fits the type it's used on, and that fields with the same response key do not conflict.
takeaways: Fragments name reusable selections on a type
Aliases are needed for the same field with different arguments
Colocate fragments with the components that render them
pitfalls: Requesting the same field twice with different arguments without aliases: a validation conflict.

quiz.q: Why must `image(width: 200)` and `image(width: 1600)` in one selection use aliases?
options: Both would map to the same response key with different values
quiz.explain: Response keys must be unambiguous, so differing arguments under one key are a conflict.

concepts.name: Interfaces and unions
concepts.summary: Model fields that can return several kinds of object, with interfaces (shared fields) and unions (one of several types).
concepts.why: Search results, activity feeds and look-ups by id often return a mix of object types.
concepts.body:
An **interface** declares fields that several object types share; each type `implements` it and must include those fields:

```graphql
interface Node { id: ID! }
type User implements Node { id: ID!  name: String! }
type Post implements Node { id: ID!  title: String! }
```

A **union** says a value is one of several object types that need not share any fields: `union SearchResult = User | Post | Tag`.

Querying a field that can return several types:

- Fields declared on an interface can be selected directly.
- Type-specific fields need an inline fragment `... on Post { title }`.
- For a union you can only select the built-in `__typename` directly; everything else goes through fragments.

On the server, GraphQL must be told which exact type each value is. In graphql-tools style resolver maps you add `__resolveType(obj)` on the interface or union, returning the type name; alternatively types can define `isTypeOf`.

Choose an interface when types truly share a contract you will query generically; choose a union for "one of these unrelated things" such as search results or a mutation result that is either a success or one of several error types. Interfaces can also implement other interfaces.
takeaways: Interface = shared fields; union = one of unrelated types
Use `... on Type` for type-specific fields
Servers need `__resolveType` (or `isTypeOf`) for abstract types
pitfalls: Forgetting `__resolveType`, which makes every polymorphic field fail at runtime.

quiz.q: On a union field, what can you select without an inline fragment?
options: Any field of the first member
The fields shared by all members
quiz.explain: Unions declare no fields of their own, so only the built-in `__typename` is available directly.

concepts.name: Errors and partial results
concepts.summary: Read the errors array, understand how null propagates through non-null fields, and decide what errors belong in the schema.
concepts.why: GraphQL responses can be partly successful, and clients must handle that correctly.
concepts.body:
A GraphQL response can contain both `data` and `errors`. Each error has a `message`, usually `locations` and a `path` to the field that failed, plus optional `extensions` for codes a program can check (e.g. `{"code": "FORBIDDEN"}`).

When a resolver throws, the executor records an error and sets that field to `null`. If the field is **nullable**, the rest of the response survives. If it is **non-null**, the null **propagates** to the nearest nullable parent, erasing the siblings too; if nothing is nullable all the way up, `data` itself becomes `null`.

That is why nullability is a design decision:

- Nullable fields keep a failure contained (a broken recommendations service does not kill the page).
- Non-null fields simplify client code, but one error then wipes out more of the response.

Two categories of errors:

- **Request errors** (a malformed document, a validation failure, bad variables): nothing executes; the response has `errors` and no `data` key.
- **Field errors** during execution: partial data plus `errors`.

For expected domain outcomes ("email taken", "not found"), many teams return typed results instead, e.g. a union (a type that is one of several listed types) `CreateUserResult = User | EmailTaken`, so client code must handle each case explicitly. Don't send the inside details of a crash (file names, the chain of function calls that failed) to clients: in production, replace unexpected error messages with a generic one.
takeaways: Errors carry message, locations, path and optional extensions
A null in a non-null field bubbles up to the nearest nullable parent
Model expected outcomes as types; reserve `errors` for failures
pitfalls: Clients that ignore `errors` whenever `data` is present and silently show incomplete screens.

quiz.q: `recommendations` were `[String!]!` instead of `[String!]` and its resolver throws. What happens to `me`?
options: The whole HTTP request fails with 500
quiz.explain: The non-null field cannot be null, so the null propagates to its nullable parent `me`.

concepts.name: GraphQL over HTTP and clients
concepts.summary: Send operations as JSON over POST or GET, read the response format, and know what client libraries add on top.
concepts.why: Every GraphQL client, from fetch to Apollo, speaks this simple HTTP protocol.
concepts.body:
GraphQL over HTTP is standardized by the GraphQL foundation's GraphQL-over-HTTP specification. A request is normally a **POST** (the HTTP method for sending data to a server) with a JSON body:

`{"query": "...", "operationName": "Book", "variables": {"id": "b1"}}`

Send `Content-Type: application/json` and `Accept: application/graphql-response+json, application/json`. Queries (never mutations) may also be sent as **GET**, the method for plain reads, with `query` and `variables` packed into the URL. Shared web caches (CDNs) can then store the answer.

Status codes: servers that answer with the newer `application/graphql-response+json` content type (the label saying what kind of data the body holds) return 4xx for requests that fail before execution (parse or validation errors), and 200 when execution started, even if some fields errored. With classic `application/json`, 200 is used for nearly everything, so clients must always inspect the `errors` array.

A plain `fetch` is enough for scripts. Client libraries add a lot:

- **Normalized caching** by `__typename` + `id` (Apollo Client, urql's graphcache, Relay).
- Generating TypeScript types from the schema and your operations (for example with `graphql-codegen`), so your editor knows the shape of every response.
- Helpers for loading long lists page by page, automatic retries of failed requests, and live updates (subscriptions, covered later).

Servers commonly offer GraphiQL at the same URL during development. **Introspection** is the built-in query that returns the whole schema; it's what lets GraphiQL autocomplete. Turn both off or restrict them in production if your schema is private.
takeaways: POST JSON with query, operationName and variables
GET is allowed for queries and enables HTTP caching
Always check `errors`, even on HTTP 200
pitfalls: Sending mutations over GET: servers must reject them, or a link on another site could make a logged-in user's browser change data (CSRF).

quiz.q: Which operations may be sent with HTTP GET?
quiz.explain: GET must be safe, so servers execute only query operations sent via GET.

concepts.name: N+1 queries and DataLoader
concepts.summary: Recognize the N+1 problem caused by per-field resolvers and fix it with per-request batching and caching via DataLoader.
concepts.why: Without batching, one innocent-looking query can trigger hundreds of database calls.
concepts.body:
Resolvers run per object. Fetch 50 books and select `author { name }`, and the naive `Book.author` resolver runs 50 separate lookups: one query for the list plus **N** for the authors, the classic **N+1 problem**.

**DataLoader** (the `dataloader` package, also ported to most languages) fixes it. You create a loader with a **batch function** that takes an array of keys and returns a promise of values in the same order. Resolvers call `loader.load(key)`; the loader collects every key requested in the same tick of the event loop and calls the batch function once.

Rules that keep it correct:

- The batch function must return exactly one result per key, **in key order** (use `null` or an `Error` for misses).
- Create loaders **per request** (in the function that builds `context`). A loader remembers every key it has loaded; shared across requests, that memory would serve out-of-date data and leak data between users with different permissions.
- Loaders cache by key within the request, so the same author loaded twice hits the database once.

Batching works because promise callbacks run as microtasks: DataLoader waits until the resolvers that are running now have all called `load`, then sends one batch. Alternatives: load the related data in the parent resolver by reading ahead in `info`, or use tools like Hasura and PostGraphile that turn a whole query into one database query.
takeaways: N+1: one query for the list plus one per item
DataLoader batches keys requested in the same tick
Batch functions return results in key order
One loader instance per request
pitfalls: A global DataLoader shared across requests: out-of-date data and leaks between users.

quiz.q: Why must DataLoader instances be created per request?
options: They can't be used from several threads
Their cache would leak data across users and go out of date
quiz.explain: A loader's cache of loaded keys is meant to live only as long as one request.

concepts.name: Pagination and connections
concepts.summary: Page through lists with offset or cursor arguments, and use the Relay connection pattern with edges and pageInfo.
concepts.why: Any list that can grow needs pagination designed into the schema from day one.
concepts.body:
Never expose an unbounded list such as `posts: [Post!]!` on a growing collection. Two styles exist:

- **Offset**: `posts(limit: 20, offset: 40)`. Simple, supports jumping to page 7, but items shift when rows are inserted, and large offsets are slow in most databases.
- **Cursor**: `posts(first: 20, after: "cursor")`. The **cursor** is an opaque string — clients pass it back without reading it — often the last item's sort value written in base64. It stays correct when items are inserted, and the database can jump straight to "items after this one" instead of counting past skipped rows.

The widely used **connection pattern** (from Relay, now a general convention) standardizes cursors:

```graphql
type PostConnection { edges: [PostEdge!]!  pageInfo: PageInfo!  totalCount: Int }
type PostEdge { node: Post!  cursor: String! }
type PageInfo { hasNextPage: Boolean!  endCursor: String  hasPreviousPage: Boolean!  startCursor: String }
```

Clients request `first`/`after` to go forward or `last`/`before` to go back. Edges are a place for relationship data (e.g. `role` on a team membership edge). Many APIs also add a `nodes` shortcut field.

Server tips: cap `first` (reject or clamp values above, say, 100), make cursors opaque so you can change their encoding, and implement that "items after this one" lookup (keyset pagination: `WHERE (created_at, id) < (...)`) rather than translating cursors back into offsets.
takeaways: Cursor pagination is stable under inserts; offset is not
Connections: edges { cursor node } plus pageInfo
Cap page sizes and keep cursors opaque
pitfalls: Returning unbounded lists that keep growing until responses take too long and time out.

quiz.q: A client has `pageInfo.endCursor = "Y3Vy"`. How does it fetch the next page?
quiz.explain: Forward pagination passes the previous end cursor as `after`.

concepts.name: Subscriptions and incremental delivery
concepts.summary: Push real-time events to clients with subscription operations over WebSockets or server-sent events.
concepts.why: Chat, notifications and live dashboards need server-pushed updates.
concepts.body:
A **subscription** is a long-lived operation: the client subscribes once and receives a stream of results, one per event. Each subscription operation must have exactly one root field.

```graphql
subscription OnMessage($room: ID!) { messageAdded(room: $room) { id text author { name } } }
```

Server side, a subscription field has a `subscribe` function returning an **async iterator** of events, and an optional `resolve` that maps each event to the field value. For every event, the selection set is executed like a normal query, so nested resolvers and loaders work as usual.

Transport is not in the core spec. The common choices:

- The **graphql-ws** protocol over a **WebSocket**, a connection that stays open so either side can send at any time (the `graphql-ws` library; the older `subscriptions-transport-ws` is deprecated).
- **Server-sent events** (graphql-sse): an ordinary HTTP response that stays open while the server keeps writing to it. It passes more easily through proxies (servers that relay traffic) and HTTP/2.

In production you run several copies of the server, so events usually come from a **pub/sub** system (Redis, Kafka, Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY): any copy publishes an event to a named channel, and every subscribed copy receives it and delivers it to its own connected clients. Check who the user is once, when the connection opens, not on every message, and re-check permissions on sensitive events.

Related but different: the `@defer` and `@stream` directives (experimental in graphql-js 17 via `experimentalExecuteIncrementally`, and supported by some servers) send one query's result in increments so slow fields arrive later. Use subscriptions for events, and simply re-asking every so often (polling) for data that changes rarely.
takeaways: Subscriptions stream one result per event
`subscribe` returns an async iterator; `resolve` maps events
Use graphql-ws or SSE; fan out events via pub/sub
pitfalls: Keeping events in one server's memory (a local event emitter), which breaks as soon as you run two server copies.

quiz.q: How many root fields may a subscription operation select?
quiz.explain: The spec requires a single root field so each event maps to one stream.

concepts.name: Evolving a schema without versions
concepts.summary: Add fields freely, deprecate before removing, use @oneOf inputs, and track which clients use what.
concepts.why: GraphQL APIs are expected to evolve continuously instead of shipping /v2.
concepts.body:
GraphQL APIs rarely publish a new numbered version (`/v2`) of their URL. Instead the schema evolves continuously, relying on one fact: clients receive only the fields they ask for, so **adding** is safe.

Safe changes: new types, new fields, new optional arguments, new enum values (if clients handle unknown values). **Breaking changes**, which make existing clients fail: removing or renaming fields, making a nullable field non-null in input positions, making an output field nullable (clients may not expect null), adding a required argument.

Removing things politely:

- Mark it `@deprecated(reason: "Use fullName")`. Introspection reports this, and editors show the field struck through. Since the September 2025 spec edition, deprecation also applies to arguments and input fields.
- Measure usage. Field-level usage reporting (Apollo GraphOS, Hive and others) tells you when nobody requests it anymore.
- Remove it once traffic is zero, and run schema checks in your automated build (CI) to catch accidental breaks.

Input design got a new tool in the September 2025 spec: **OneOf input objects**. `input UserBy @oneOf { id: ID  email: String }` requires exactly one field to be set, replacing hand-written checks and letting one argument accept "one of these ways to identify a user".

Design for the client: name fields after domain concepts rather than database columns, prefer specific fields to generic JSON blobs, and avoid exposing internal IDs or implementation details you might want to change.
takeaways: Adding fields is safe because clients select what they need
Deprecate, measure usage, then remove
`@oneOf` inputs require exactly one field
Run breaking-change checks in CI
pitfalls: Changing a field's type in place instead of adding a new field and deprecating the old one.

quiz.q: Which change is breaking for existing clients?
options: Adding a new field to a type
quiz.explain: Existing queries that select the old name would fail validation.

concepts.name: Parse, validate, execute
concepts.summary: Follow a request through graphql-js: parsing to an AST, validation rules, coercion and execution with completion.
concepts.why: Knowing the steps lets you write custom checks, cache work between requests and debug odd behaviour.
concepts.body:
Every GraphQL server handles a request in the same three steps from the spec, which graphql-js exposes as separate functions:

- `parse(source)` turns the text into a **document AST** (abstract syntax tree): a tree of objects such as `OperationDefinition`, `Field` and `FragmentSpread`, each with its position in the text. The same text always gives the same tree, so servers cache ASTs by a hash of the query.
- `validate(schema, document, rules)` runs the **validation rules** (fields exist, arguments typed, fragments used, no conflicting response keys, variables defined...). You can add rules, e.g. a max-depth rule. Validation is also cacheable per schema and document.
- `execute({ schema, document, variableValues, contextValue })` converts variables to their declared types, then **collects fields** (merging fragments and same-named fields), resolves them, and **completes** values: serializing scalars, mapping lists, resolving abstract types, and enforcing non-null.

Execution details experts rely on:

- Top-level query fields may run at the same time; top-level mutation fields run one after another.
- Field collection merges selections with the same response key, so `{ a: f  a: f }` resolves once.
- The `info` argument contains `fieldNodes`, `returnType`, `path` and `fragments`, enough to look ahead and build an optimal database query.
- `graphql()` is just parse + validate + execute in one call.

Tooling builds on the AST: `visit()` walks and transforms documents, `print()` turns an AST back into text, and `TypeInfo` tracks types during a visit.
takeaways: Steps: parse to an AST, validate with rules, execute and complete
Parsing and validation are cacheable per document
Field collection merges fields with the same response key
`info` exposes the selection for looking ahead
pitfalls: Re-parsing and re-validating identical documents on every request in busy servers.

quiz.q: A query selects `a` directly and again through a fragment. How many times does the resolver for `a` run?
options: Zero, it is a conflict error
It depends on what runs at the same time
quiz.explain: Field collection merges selections with the same response key before resolving.

concepts.name: Securing a GraphQL API
concepts.summary: Defend against expensive queries with depth and cost limits, trusted documents, time limits and per-field permission checks.
concepts.why: A flexible query language also lets attackers write very expensive requests.
concepts.body:
GraphQL lets a client write any query the schema allows, so a public API needs limits. A REST API gets some of these for free, because each fixed URL does a known amount of work.

**Query cost.** Nested lists multiply: `users(first: 100) { friends(first: 100) { friends(first: 100) { name } } }` asks for a million objects. Defences, usually added as extra validation rules or server plugins:

- Maximum **depth** and maximum number of fields / aliases (aliases can repeat an expensive field many times in one request).
- **Cost analysis**: assign weights per field and multiply by list-size arguments; reject queries over a budget. Also limit batching (several operations sent in one HTTP request).
- Execution **timeouts**, and per-client rate limits (caps on how much each caller may do) based on cost, not request count.

**Trusted documents** (persisted operations): for first-party clients, register every operation when the app is built and let the server accept only their hashes. This shuts down arbitrary queries entirely and shrinks request size. Automatic persisted queries (APQ) are a caching optimisation, not a security feature, since anyone can register a query.

**Authorization** belongs in the business layer and must be checked on every field or object that needs it: an object reachable through a nested path is just as exposed as a root field. Use the per-request context for the user identity.

Also: hiding introspection and detailed errors is only an extra layer (the schema leaks through your apps anyway). Cap the size of request bodies, and block CSRF by requiring a JSON content type or a custom header on POST requests.
takeaways: Limit depth, aliases, batch size and estimated cost
Trusted documents allow only pre-registered operations
Authorize in the business layer, on every reachable object
Hiding introspection is not a security boundary
pitfalls: Checking permissions only on root fields while the same data is reachable through nested relations.

quiz.q: Why is automatic persisted queries (APQ) not a security measure?
options: Any client can register arbitrary queries
quiz.explain: APQ registers whatever hash a client sends; only build-time trusted documents restrict operations.

concepts.name: Federation and distributed graphs
concepts.summary: Compose one supergraph from many team-owned subgraphs, and know the trade-offs versus schema stitching or a monolith.
concepts.why: Large organisations split one GraphQL API across many services and teams.
concepts.body:
One GraphQL schema for a whole company slows everyone down when dozens of teams own the data and must coordinate every change. **Federation** lets each team run a **subgraph**, a normal GraphQL service declaring the types it owns, while a **router** (a gateway server in front of them) exposes the combined **supergraph** to clients.

The core idea is **entities**: types that several subgraphs contribute fields to, identified by a key. In Apollo Federation:

```graphql
# products subgraph
type Product @key(fields: "upc") { upc: ID!  name: String!  price: Int! }
# reviews subgraph
type Product @key(fields: "upc") { upc: ID!  reviews: [Review!]! }
```

Composition checks that subgraphs agree and produces a supergraph schema. At runtime the router builds a **query plan**: fetch from products, then send the `upc` keys to reviews through the special `_entities` field, then merge.

The GraphQL Foundation's Composite Schemas working group is standardizing these ideas vendor-neutrally; implementations include Apollo Federation (Router), WunderGraph Cosmo, Grafbase and The Guild's Hive Gateway.

Trade-offs: federation adds an extra network hop, query planning, and a schema registry plus composition checks in your automated build (CI). An N+1 problem across subgraphs turns into batching entity look-ups. Choose it for organisational scale; a single well-modularised server is simpler for one team. Schema stitching is an older, more manual alternative.
takeaways: Subgraphs own types; a router serves the composed supergraph
Entities with `@key` are extended across subgraphs
Composition and schema checks run in CI
Adopt for team scale, not for small apps
pitfalls: Federating a small single-team API and paying the operational cost for nothing.

quiz.q: How does a router fetch `reviews` for a Product owned by another subgraph?
options: It sends entity representations (keys) to the reviews subgraph
quiz.explain: The planner passes `@key` values to the `_entities` field of the subgraph that adds the field.
